quotes.quote: The blind cave tetra was discovered by the ornamental fish collector C. Basil Jordan in a cave in the state of San Luis Potosí in Mexico.

sections.html: The blind cave tetra was discovered by the ornamental fish collector C. Basil Jordan in a cave in the state of San Luis Potosí in Mexico. Jordan collected 100 specimens and brought them to the USA without losing a single one. It was the first cave species of the tetra family ever found.
Blind cave tetras can be kept with any type of peaceful fish. Their blindness is no handicap at all.

The species was described in a new genus under the name Anoptichthys jordani, which translates as "Jordan's eyeless fish". It proved to be very hardy and easy to breed.

The blind cave tetra can be crossed over generations with the normal-looking tetra Astyanax fasciatus mexicanus, which lives in surface waters all over Mexico. For this reason many scientists argued that the blind cave tetra is not a species of its own. Most recent scientists accept species concepts based more on evolutionary aspects, and so the blind cave tetra is now most often named Astyanax jordani.

The species has never died out in aquaria since the first importation in 1936, and the ancestors of all specimens kept today are descended from the 100 originally wild-collected fish. Fish currently available were bred in Singapore, but they also belong to the aquarium population established in 1936.

Most probably this is why aquarists keep breeding them: most fish enthusiasts want to study the unique adaptation of the blind cave tetra once in their lifetime.
